# On the Holy Prayer

...and have ordained [it] for the will of your figures and creatures; lead me back again in Christ my Savior into my former glory.

And although the body in this time is not worthy of it, because it has become a stinking corpse <note>original Latin: "Cadaver." This term emphasizes the decay and corruption of the physical body in its fallen state, contrasted with the "noble mind."</note>: yet enlighten my noble <term>mind</term> <note>original: "Gemühte." As established on previous pages, this refers to the inner core of a person where the soul and intellect meet.</note> as your image, and let it dwell in Christ my Savior, in heaven, in the fellowship of your holy angels.

Place it in the midday of your wonders, for which you have formed it, and rule, O Lord Jesus Christ, as over your inheritance, with it over all things. And help me to be humble, and not to take credit for what you do, but to look to you, and may my desire praise you, and live constantly in your <term>harmony</term> <note>original: "Harmoni." In mystical thought, this is the perfect, musical resonance of the divine order.</note>, and without you desire to begin or do nothing.

O Lord, you holiest light, let my mind dwell in your forecourts, so that it may rejoice in your brilliance which flows out from you, and never depart from you again eternally; but lead it back to the fellowship of the holy angels, to which you have ordained us.

O holy name <term>Emanuel</term> <note>original Hebrew-derived: "Emanuel." Meaning "God with us," used here as a meditative focus on Christ’s presence.</note>, it is yours; do with it what you will, Amen.

## Concerning the Descent of the <term>Mind</term> <note>original: "Gemüht." A central term in German mysticism referring to the soul’s deep-seated disposition or inner spiritual core.</note>

O **GOD**, how miserable, full of lamentation, grief, and worry is our time, full of anguish and tribulation! When we think we stand upright and wish to rejoice in the work of our hands, you overshadow us with your wrath <note>original: "Grim." Refers to fierce anger or divine indignation.</note> and cause us to be anxious. We run and are afraid, and there is no one chasing us except your wrath into our destruction. We consume our days like idle chatter; like a speech that is forgotten, so our days pass away, and we are forever in unrest. Unsteady is our conduct; we rely on our own arm and cling to the works of our hands and do not trust you entirely. Therefore you let us pass away in our anguish and torment. We never consider that you, O **GOD**, work and do everything yourself; for no breath can stir without you, and no blade of grass can crown the earth without you. We see all this, yet we build upon our vanity, upon the work of our hands, and do not trust you rightly. We gather and do not enjoy it; a stranger torments himself therein with vanity, and there is no end to the misery that we practice.

O **GOD**, remember our toil and misery, and turn your wrath and curse from us. And let us run again toward your goal, so that we may return to our inheritance and rejoice in your wonders. ### The 1st Chapter.

Whoever thinks to work anything perfect and good, in which he hopes to rejoice eternally and to enjoy it, let him depart from <term>selfhood</term> <note>original: "Selbheit". # On the New Birth.

---

...[if] we only believe it has happened; rather, it must be an inborn, childlike birth. <note>Böhme is critiquing "historical faith"—merely believing the facts of the Bible—and insisting on a literal internal transformation.</note> Just as the flesh must die, so also must the life and the will of **sin** die; and one must become like a child that knows nothing, and only sighs for the **Mother** who gave it birth. <note>In Böhme’s theology, the "Mother" often represents the Divine Wisdom (Sophia) or the Spirit of Christ from which the soul is reborn.</note> Thus, a **Christian’s** will must enter back into the **Mother**—that is, into the **Spirit of Christ**—and in that self-sameness <note>original: "Selbeheit"</note> of **self-will** and capacity, become a child. There, the will and the desire are directed only toward the **Mother**; and out of the **Spirit of Christ**, a new will and obedience must rise from death in **righteousness**, which no longer wills **sin**.

For the will that allows **vanity** <note>original: "Eitelkeit"; refers to the transitory, empty nature of the worldly life.</note> into itself and desires it is not **born again**; and yet, in those who are **born again**, there remains a will that longs for **vanity** and sins. Therefore, we must rightly consider the image of man and how the new **regeneration** occurs. For it does not happen in the mortal flesh, yet it truly happens in us, in **flesh and blood**, in **water and spirit**, as the **Scripture** says.

So we must rightly consider what kind of man is in us who is a **member of Christ** and a **temple of GOD**, dwelling in heaven; and then what kind of man that is whom the **Devil** rules and drives. He cannot drive the **temple of Christ**; nor does he care much for the mortal flesh; and yet there are not three people within one another, but only a single one.

<summary>Böhme describes the "New Birth" as a literal internal death of the sinful self-will, requiring the believer to become like a helpless child dependent on the Spirit of Christ. He introduces the central paradox of the Christian life: that a single person can simultaneously be a temple of God and a mortal being prone to worldly vanity.</summary>

### The Fifth Book

---

If we now wish to consider this, we must contemplate **Time** and **Eternity**, and how these are within one another; furthermore, **Light** and **Darkness**, **Good** and **Evil**: but especially the **original state** <note>original: "Urstand"; refers to the primal, foundational state of being before manifestation.</note> and source of **Man**.

->This is now to be considered thus:<-

<margin>+</margin>We look at the external world, with the stars and the four **elements**, in which **man** and all **creatures** live: this is not, nor is it called, **God**. **God** indeed dwells within it, but the essence of the external world does not comprehend <note>original: "begreifft"; carries the dual meaning of "containing" and "understanding."</note> Him. We also see how the **light** shines in the **darkness**, and the **darkness** does not comprehend the **light**, yet one dwells within the other. We also have an example of this in the four **elements**, which in their **original state** are only one element, and that is neither hot nor cold, neither dry nor wet; yet it divides itself through movement into four properties: namely, into **Fire**, **Air**, **Water**, and **Earth**.

Who would believe that **fire** could give birth to **water**? And that the **original state** of **fire** could be in **water**? If we did not see this with our own eyes in the **heat-lightning**, and also find it in living beings: that the **essential fire** <note>In Böhme’s alchemy, "essential fire" is the life-force or spiritual heat that animates physical matter.</note> dwells in the **body** <note>original: "Corpore" (Latin)</note>, in the **blood**, and that the **blood** is its **mother**; and the **fire** is the **father** of the **blood**.

And just as **GOD** now dwells in the world and fills all things, and yet possesses <note>In the sense of "owning" or being limited by the material nature of the thing possessed.</note> nothing: and the **fire** in the wat— <meta>catchword: water</meta>

He introduces the "essential fire" in the blood as a microcosm of how the spiritual resides within the material.</summary>

# The Fifth Book

### How the Fiery Dark-Anguish is Transformed into a Joy.

For, just as the nature of anguish in the darkness is a cause of sadness: So it is in the light a cause of outward and moving joy. For the <term>torment<gloss>original: "Quaal"; Böhme uses this to describe the active, vibrating quality of a spiritual force, which can be experienced as pain or as intense joy.</gloss></term> in the light, and the torment in the darkness, is but one eternal torment, only one nature. Just as fire and light are but one nature, and yet produce a vast difference in the torment; one dwells in the other, and generates the other, and yet is not the other. The fire is painful and consuming, and the light is giving, friendly, powerful, and rich in joy—a lovely delight.

Thus also man is to be considered by us: He sees and lives in three worlds; the one is the eternal Dark-World, as the <term>center<gloss>original: "Centrum"; in Böhme’s mystical physics, this is the point of origin or the heart where spiritual forces are first birthed.</gloss></term> of eternal nature, which brings forth the fire as the <term>anguish-torment<gloss>original: "Angst-Quaal"; Böhme’s signature term for the soul’s inner state of restless, grinding conflict when it is separated from the divine light.</gloss></term>. And the other is the eternal Light-World, which generates eternal joy, which is the Divine Dwelling-place, wherein the Spirit of God dwells, into which the Spirit of Christ takes on human essence <note>original: "Menschlich Wesen"; referring to the Incarnation, where the divine nature takes on a human form.</note> and drives away the darkness, so that it must be a cause of joy in the Spirit of Christ, in the light. The third world is the outer visible one, in the four elements and the visible stars: Although every element has a star within it according to its <term>property<gloss>original: "Eigenschafft"; the inherent character or specific quality that defines how a thing behaves and what it desires.</gloss></term>, from which desire and quality arise, like a mind.

<summary>Böhme explains that joy and sadness come from the same source of spiritual "torment," differing only by the presence or absence of light. He outlines the "Three Worlds" (Dark, Light, and External) that coexist within the human soul.</summary>

# Of Regeneration.

Adam could not give birth magically, because his desire entered into vanity.

Thus Moses says: *And he caused a deep sleep to fall upon him, and he fell asleep.* That is: Because he did not wish to remain in obedience to the Divine Harmony, within those properties where he should have stood still as an instrument for the Spirit of GOD; so He allowed him to fall from the Divine Harmony into a self-made harmony, namely, into the awakened properties of good and evil; and into these the soulful spirit entered.

There, in this sleep, he died to the angelic world and fell prey to the outward **Fiat** <note>original: "Fiat"; the creative command "Let there be"</note>: and it was now all over for the eternal image according to God's generation. Out of him, out of one body, He made two: and divided the properties of the **tinctures** <term>original: "Tincturen"; spiritual infusions or essences that give life and specific quality to matter</term>, such as the watery and fiery constellations within the Element—not entirely in their physical essence, but in spirit: namely, as the properties of the watery and fiery soul, though it is but one; yet the property of the **tincture** was separated. Adam’s own love-desire was taken from him and formed into a woman after his own likeness. And for this reason, the man now desires the woman’s **matrix** <term>here referring to the receptive, nurturing principle</term> so intensely: and the woman desires the man’s **limbus** <term>original: "Limbum"; the masculine, fiery essence or "seed" of the soul</term>, as the fire-

### Chapter 5.

<margin>+</margin>
Furthermore, a Christian should now consider why he calls himself a Christian, and reflect carefully on whether he truly is one. For, merely learning to know and understand that I am a sinner, and that Christ has put my sin to death on the Cross and shed His blood for me—that does not yet make me a Christian. The inheritance belongs only to the children. A servant-girl in the house knows well what her mistress likes, but that does not make her an heir to her mistress's property. The devil also knows that there is a God, but that does not make him an angel again. However, if the servant-girl in the house marries the mistress’s son, she may well come into the inheritance of the mistress's property.

<margin>/</margin>
This is also how it should be understood in our Christianity: The **children of history** <term>original: "Historien-Kinder"; those who possess an intellectual or "historical" faith—believing the facts of the Bible—without undergoing an internal spiritual transformation</term> are not heirs to the treasures of Christ; rather, the **legitimate children** <note>original: "Eheliche Kinder," referring to those born of the spiritual marriage between the soul and the Spirit of Christ</note> are those who are born anew from Christ’s Spirit. For God said to Abraham: *Cast out the son of the servant-woman; he shall not inherit with the son of the free woman* <note>A reference to Genesis 21:10 regarding Ishmael and Isaac, used here as an allegory for the fleshly versus the spiritual mind</note>; for he was a mocker, and only a "son of history"—not a son of the faith and spirit of Abraham.

# The Fifth Book

That same inborn <term>essence <note>original: "Essentz"; in this context, it refers to the fundamental spiritual substance or inner nature of a person.</note></term> is not of this world, but in heaven, of which **St. Paul** says: "Our way of life <note>original: "Wandel"; often translated in Bibles of this era as "citizenship" or "conversation," referring to one's conduct and place of belonging.</note> is in heaven." The child-like essence walks in heaven, and heaven is within the person. But if heaven is not open within a person, and he only stands before heaven acting hypocritically, saying: "I am still on the outside, but **CHRIST** will receive me out of grace; his merit is indeed mine"—such a person, according to the outward man, exists in vanity and sin, and his soul is in hell, as if in **God’s** wrath.

<margin>+</margin> Therefore, learn to understand rightly what **Christ** has taught and done for us. He is our heaven; he must take shape <note>original: "eine Gestalt gewinnen"; meaning to become a formed, living reality within the soul.</note> within us if we are to be in heaven. In this way, the inner man of the soul, together with the holy body of **Christ**, is in heaven—as in the New Birth—while the outward mortal man is in the world. Of this **Christ** says: "My sheep are in my hand; no one can pluck them out of my hand. The Father who gave them to me is greater than all."

A beast goes into the churches and to the Lord’s Supper, and a beast leaves again. How can he eat, who has no mouth? How can he hear, who has no hearing? Can one enjoy a food that is locked away from his mouth? How can he drink, who is far from the water? What does it help me to go into the walled church and fill my ears with an empty breath? Or go to the Lord’s Supper and feed only the earthly mouth, which is mortal and perishable? I might as well give it a piece of bread at home so that it would be full.

## Of Rebirth.

...and brings forth godless fruits, from which the world has become a murderer's den of the Devil, so that within both the teacher and the listener, there is nothing but vain mockery, blasphemy, derision, word-wrangling, and snapping at one another.

The holy person has his church within himself, wherein he hears and teaches. But Babel <note>In Böhme’s writing, "Babel" refers to the "City of Confusion," signifying the institutionalized, sectarian, and spiritually empty churches of his time.</note> has a heap of stones; she goes in there to play the hypocrite and put on a show; she lets herself be seen in beautiful clothes and acts devout and pious. The **stone church** <term>stone church <note>original: "steinerne Kirche"; the physical building of the church as opposed to the "living temple" of the human heart.</note></term> is her god, in which she places her trust. The holy person, however, has his church with him and in him in all places: whether he stands or walks, lies down or sits, he is in his church; he is in the true Christian church, in the temple of Christ. The Holy Spirit preaches to him from all creatures; in everything he looks upon, he sees a preacher of God.

Here the mocker will say that I despise the stone church where the congregation gathers. To that I say no! ## The VII. Chapter.

<margin>+ . . ,</margin>
A true person who is born anew in the Spirit of Christ exists in the simplicity of Christ and has no quarrel with anyone over religion. He has enough struggle within himself against his own animalistic, evil flesh and blood. He always considers himself a great sinner and stands in fear before God. But the love of Christ breaks through and drives it out, just as the day swallows up the night.

But for the ungodly, his sins rest in the sleep of death, sprout up from the abyss, and bear fruit in hell.

The letters all stand in one root, and that root is the Spirit of God. Just as various flowers all stand in the earth and grow alongside one another: none bites the other over colors, scent, or taste. They allow the earth and sun, as well as rain and wind, heat and cold, to do with them as they will, yet each one grows in its own essence <term>essence <note>original: "Essentz"; the fundamental spiritual substance or inner nature of a being.</note></term> and quality. So it is also with the children of God; they have various gifts and knowledge <term>knowledge <note>original: "Erkantnüß"; an experiential, living realization of God rather than mere intellectual learning.</note></term>, but all from one Spirit.

### Chapter VIII.

<margin>1. 2. 3. 4.</margin> The entire Christian religion consists in this: that we learn to know ourselves—what we are, where we have come from, how we have entered from unity <term>unity<note>original: "Einigung"; refers to a state of being "at one" with God’s will before the fall of man.</note></term> into disunity, and how we have awakened this discord within ourselves. Secondly: where we were when we were in unity, back when we were children of **GOD**. Thirdly: how we are now in disunity, in strife and ill-will. Fourthly: where we are journeying to after leaving this fragile existence—where we intend to go with the immortal part of us, and also with the mortal.

<margin>† //</margin> In these four points lies our whole religion: to learn how to come out of disunity and vanity, and to enter again into the one tree from which we all came in Adam—which is **Christ** in us. We need not quarrel about anything, nor do we have any cause for strife. Let each person only practice how he may enter again into the love of **GOD** and of his brother.

The Testaments of Christ <note>original: "Christi Testamenta"; Böhme uses the Latin plural to refer to the legacy of Christ's teachings and the sacraments.</note> are absolutely nothing else than a brotherly covenant: that **God** binds Himself to us in **Christ**, and we in Him. All teaching should point toward this, as should all willing, living, and doing. Whatever teaches or acts otherwise is merely Babel <note>Referring to the Tower of Babel, a symbol of human pride and the confusion of languages and sects.</note> and a fable; it is merely a handiwork of pride <term>pride<note>original: "Hoffart"; specifically refers to the spiritual arrogance of "knowing" better than others.</note></term>, a useless judgment, a confusing of the world, and a hypocrisy of the devil, with which he blinds simplicity.

<meta>catchword: Everything</meta>

<summary>Böhme defines the Christian life as a four-step process of self-recognition and a return to spiritual unity, arguing that all religious doctrine is useless if it does not lead to brotherly love and union with Christ.</summary>

### The Fifth Booklet

<margin>+</margin> …a teacher of the letter, a knower of histories, and not of the Spirit of **GOD** in **Christ**. Everything with which one intends to serve **GOD** must happen in faith, as in the Spirit; this makes the work complete and pleasing to God. Whatever a person begins and does in faith, they do in the Spirit of **GOD**, who works within the work; that is pleasing to **GOD**, for He has made it Himself, and His power is within it; it is holy.

But what is done in selfhood <term>selfhood<note>original: "Selbheit"; a central concept in Böhme’s writing referring to the prideful, ego-driven state of a human soul that has turned away from God to serve its own desires.</note></term> without faith is only a **figure** <note>original: "Figur"; here meaning an empty outward form or a mere representation lacking the internal reality.</note> or a husk of a true Christian work.

If you serve your brother and do it only out of hypocrisy <term>hypocrisy<note>original: "Gleißnerey"; in 17th-century German, this word implies a "false glitter" or a deceptive outward show of piety.</note></term>, and give to him unwillingly, then you do not serve **GOD**. For your faith does not go forth out of love into hope within your gift. You may well serve your brother, and he for his part thanks **GOD** and also blesses you for his part; but you do not bless him, for you give him a grumbling spirit within your gift, which does not enter into **GOD’s** Spirit, into the hope of faith. Therefore, your gift is only half given, and you have only a half-reward for it.

The same is to be understood regarding taking: if one gives in faith in Divine hope, he blesses his gift in his faith; but he who receives it ungratefully and grumbles in spirit, he curses it in the consumption <term>consumption<note>original: "Nießsung"; the act of using, eating, or enjoying the benefit of something received.</note></term>. Thus, to each remains his own: what he sows, that he also reaps.

<summary>Böhme argues that true service to God must be performed through the Holy Spirit and faith, rather than through mere intellectual knowledge or reluctant "good works." He emphasizes that the internal intent and spiritual state of both the giver and the receiver determine the spiritual value of an action.</summary>

## Being a Dialogue between a Master and a Disciple.
### The first Question and Answer.

<margin>1.</margin>The Disciple spoke to the Master: How may I come to the **supersensual life** <term>supersensual life<note>original: "über-sinnlichen Leben"; a life existing beyond or above the physical senses and the material world.</note></term>, so that I may see **GOD** and hear Him speak?
The Master spoke: When you can swing yourself for one moment into that where no **creature** <note>original: "Creatur"; in Böhme's thought, this refers to any finite, created thing that possesses an individual identity separate from the divine essence.</note> dwells, then you hear what **GOD** speaks.

<margin>2.</margin>The Disciple spoke: Is that near or far?
The Master spoke: It is in you; and if you can be silent for one hour from all your **willing** and **thinking** <note>original: "Sinnen"; refers here to the active, discursive thoughts and sensory processing of the mind.</note>, then you will hear the unspeakable words of **GOD**.

<margin>3.</margin>The Disciple spoke: How can I hear, if I stand still from senses and willing?
The Master spoke: When you stand still from the thinking and willing of your **selfhood** <term>selfhood<note>original: "Selbheit"; the ego-driven state of being where a person acts according to their own isolated will rather than in unity with the divine.</note></term>, then the eternal hearing, seeing, and speaking becomes manifest in you, and **God** hears and sees through you: your own hearing, wil-

<summary>This page introduces Jacob Böhme’s mystical dialogue on how to achieve "supersensual" perception by silencing the individual ego and will. The Master explains that God is heard only when one transcends the realm of created things and enters a state of spiritual stillness.</summary>
<keywords>supersensual life, stillness, selfhood, divine voice, Jacob Böhme, mysticism, spiritual perception</keywords>

4. The Disciple spoke: With what shall I hear and see **GOD**, since He is beyond nature and **creature** <note>original: "Creatur"; Böhme uses this to refer to any individual, created being or thing in the material world.</note>?

The Master spoke: When you are quiet and silent, then you are that which **God** was before nature and creature, and out of which He made your nature and creature. Then you hear and see with that wherewith **God** saw and heard in you before your own **willing**, seeing, and hearing began.

5. The Disciple spoke: What holds me back then, so that I cannot reach it?

The Master spoke: Your own **willing**, hearing, and seeing; and that you strive against that from which you have come. With your own **willing**, you break yourself off from **God’s** will; and with your own seeing, you see only into your own **willing**. Your **willing** stops your hearing with the **self-willedness** <note>original: "Eigensinnigkeit"; the state of being trapped in one's own ego and physical senses.</note> of earthly, natural things, and leads you into a **ground** <term>ground<note>original: "Grund"; in Böhme's philosophy, this refers to the fundamental essence or foundation of being.</note></term>, and overshadows you with that which you desire, so that you cannot come to the **super-natural**, **supersensual**.

4. The Disciple spoke: With what shall I hear and see **GOD**, since He is beyond **Nature** and **Creature** <note>original: "Creatur"; refers to any created being or thing in the material world, distinct from the uncreated God.</note>?

The Master spoke: When you keep silent and still, then you are that which God was before Nature and Creature, out of which He made your nature and creature. Thus you hear and see with that which God used to see and hear in you, before your own willing, seeing, and hearing began.

5. The Disciple spoke: What then holds me back, so that I cannot reach that place?

The Master spoke: Your own willing, hearing, and seeing; and that you strive against that from which you have come. With your own willing, you break yourself off from God's will; and with your own seeing, you look only into your own willing. Your willing stops up your hearing with the **self-will** <term>self-will<note>original: "Eigensinnigkeit"; the state of being focused on one's own ego and earthly desires as a separate entity from the divine.</note></term> of earthly, natural things, and leads you into a **ground** <term>ground<note>original: "Grund"; a central term in Böhme’s mysticism referring to the foundational essence of the soul or reality.</note></term>, and shadows you with what you yourself desire, so that you cannot reach the **supernatural**, **supersensual**.

...you act as your will drives you. The third is that you subject yourself to the **Cross**, so that you may endure the temptation of **Nature** and **Creature** <note>original: "Anfechtung der Natur und Creatur"; refers to the trials, suffering, and sensory distractions inherent in being a physical being in a material world.</note>. And if you do this, **God** will speak into you, and lead your surrendered <term>surrendered<note>original: "gelassenen"; from 'Gelassenheit,' a central concept in German mysticism meaning a state of letting go of one's ego and yielding completely to the divine will.</note></term> will into Himself, into the **supernatural ground**; so you will hear what the **LORD** speaks within you.

7. **The Disciple spoke:** Must I then leave the world and my life, if I were to do that?

**The Master spoke:** If you leave the world, you enter into that from which the world was made. And if you lose your life and reach the powerlessness of your own ability, then your life stands in Him for whose sake you leave it—namely, in **God**, from whom it entered into the body.

8. **The Disciple spoke:** **God** created man for the natural life, that he might rule over every **creature** on earth and be a master over everything in this world; therefore, he must surely possess it as his own property.

**The Master spoke:** If you rule over all creatures only externally, then you exist with your will and your dominion in an **animal manner**, and you stand only in a symbolic, fleeting dominion. Furthermore, you lead your desire into an **animal essence**, by which you are infected and captured, and you even take on an animal nature. But if you have left the symbolic nature, then you stand in the **super-symbolic** <term>super-symbolic<note>original: "über-Bildigkeit"; a state of being beyond mere forms, images, or representations, reaching the eternal essence of reality.</note></term> and rule in the **ground** over all creatures from which they were created.

<summary>The Master explains that true spiritual hearing requires surrendering one's ego and enduring the "Cross" of physical life. He further argues that true dominion over the world is not found in outward possession, which leads to a beast-like nature, but in transcending forms to reach the divine essence of all things.</summary>

**The Master spoke:** Gladly; think on the words of our **Lord Jesus Christ**, when He spoke: "Unless you turn back and become like children, you shall not see **God’s** kingdom" <note>Matthew 18:3</note>. If it is now your will to become equal to all things, then you must leave all things, and turn your desire away from them. You must not crave them, nor take them upon yourself to possess as a property <term>property<note>original: "Eigenthumb"; here referring to "self-hood" or the ego's claim of ownership. In Böhme's thought, the desire to own things attaches the soul to the material world and prevents spiritual union.</note></term> that is "something." For as soon as you grasp that "Something" in your desire, and allow it into yourself and take it as your own property, then that "Something" becomes one thing with you. It works with you in your will, and you are then bound to protect it and care for it as if it were your own essence. But if you take nothing into your desire, then you are free from all things and rule over all things at once. For you have nothing in your receptivity <note>original: "Annehmligkeit"; the capacity or tendency to take things in and be affected by them.</note>, and you are a "Nothing" to all things, and all things are likewise a "Nothing" to you. You are as a child who does not understand what a thing is. And even if you do understand it, you understand it without it touching your sensitivity <note>original: "Empfindlichkeit"; the state of being emotionally or sensorially moved by external objects.</note>, in the same way that **God** rules and sees all things, yet no thing can grasp Him.

The final judgment is an ignition of the fire according to **God’s** Love and <term>Wrath<note>original: "Zorn." ## Jacob Böhme's Highly Precious Gate
->of<-
# Divine Contemplation,
->Concerning what the Great Mystery <term>Mysterium Magnum (Latin: The "Great Mystery," a term used by Böhme to describe the chaotic potential or the unmanifested source of all creation)</term> is, and how all things exist from, through,<-
->and in GOD; how GOD is so<-
->near to all things and fulfills all.<-

### The First Chapter.
### What GOD is: And how one should recognize His (the Divine) Being by His revelation.

->Reason speaks:<-

I hear many things said of God, that there is a God who has created all things, and also sustains all things, and I ask: But I have not yet seen one, or heard of one, who has seen God, or who could say: **Where God dwells or is, or what He is like?**

For when Reason looks upon the nature of this world and considers how it fares for the pious as it does for the wicked: and how all things are mortal and fragile: also how the pious man sees no savior who delivers him from the anguish and adversity of the wicked, and thus must go down to the grave <note>literally: "the pit"</note> with anxieties in misery; so it thinks that all things happen thus by chance, that there is no God who takes concern for the sufferer, because He leaves the one who hopes in Him to remain stuck in misery and go down to the grave therein, and one has also heard of no one who has come back from decay and said that he had been with God.

->Answer.<-

# On Divine Contemplation

A life of pain is an entrance into the painless, the non-suffering state.

<margin>+</margin>
In this, one rightly understands the hidden God: how He reveals Himself in the human mind <term>Gemühte (the inner seat of the soul, encompassing the mind, will, and emotions)</term>, punishes unrighteousness within the conscience, and draws the one who suffers unrighteously to Himself through that very suffering. One sees how the life of reason—as the natural life—must, through suffering, be overcome by a desire to turn back into that from which it first came. It must desire to hate itself and to die away from its natural willing, so that it might reach the supernatural.

## Reason speaks:

> Why has **GOD** created a life of painful suffering? Could it not exist in a better state without suffering and torment, since He is the ground and beginning of all things? Why does He tolerate this opposition? Why does He not break the power of evil, so that only goodness might exist in all things?

### Answer.

<margin>+ " " " /</margin>
No thing can become manifest to itself without contrariety <note>original: "Widerwertigkeit," a central term in Böhme’s thought meaning opposition or friction; he believes nothing can know itself without hitting a limit or resistance</note>. For if a thing has nothing that resists it, it always flows outward and never returns into itself. But if it does not return into itself—as into that from which it originally originated—then it knows nothing of its own original state <note>original: "Urstand," the primal condition or origin of a being</note>.

If the natural life had no contrariety and were without a goal, it would never ask after its own "ground" or origin. Thus, the hidden **GOD** would remain unknown to the natural life. Furthermore, if there were no opposition in life, there would be no sensory perception, nor any will,

<sig>A 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: len/</meta>

<summary>This page addresses the philosophical problem of why a good God allows suffering, arguing that "contrariety" or opposition is necessary for self-awareness and spiritual growth. The author explains that without the friction of suffering, the soul would never seek its divine origin or understand its own nature.</summary>
<keywords>Jacob Böhme, theodicy, suffering, contrariety, Gemüt, self-revelation, the hidden God, spiritual rebirth</keywords>

[ac]tion, nor working, nor even understanding or knowledge within it. For a thing that has only one will has no differentiation <term>Schiedlichkeit (the quality of being divided, distinct, or diverse)</term>. If it does not sense a counter-will <note>original: "Widerwillen," meaning a resisting or opposing force</note> that causes it to drive into motion, it stands still. For a unified thing knows nothing more than "One." And even if it is good in itself, it knows neither evil nor good, for it has nothing in itself that makes it perceptible.

Thus we can also philosophize about the will of God and say: If the hidden **GOD**, who is but a single Being and Will, had not led Himself out of Himself with His will; and had not led Himself out of the eternal science <term>Wissenschafft (in this context, divine wisdom or the "knowing" of God)</term> in the *temperament* <note>original: "Temperamento," referring to a state where all spiritual qualities are in perfect, harmonious balance</note>, into a differentiation of the will; and if He had not introduced this same differentiation into a tangibility <term>Infaßlichkeit (the quality of being able to be grasped, contained, or manifested in form)</term> for a natural and creaturely life; and if this same differentiation did not stand in conflict within life, how then would the hidden will of God—which in itself is only One—become manifest to Himself?

How can there be a knowledge of itself in a single, unified will? But if there is a differentiation in the single Will, so that the differentiation introduces itself into centers <term>Centra (points of focus or individual souls/entities)</term> and self-will—so that there is a self-will in that which is differentiated—then in one single Will, unfathomable and innumerable wills arise, like branches from a tree. Thus we see and understand that in such differentiation, every distinct will introduces itself into its own form, and that the conflict of the wills is about form: that one

### Chapter 11.
### Concerning the Mind, Will, and Thoughts of Human Life: how they have their original state <note>original: "Urstand," meaning the primordial source or foundation of being</note> from the Will of God, and how they are a counter-image <note>original: "Gegenwurff," a Böhmean term for an "object" or "opposition" that reflects the self, like an image in a mirror</note>, as an image of God, in which God wills, works, and dwells.

->Answer.<-

The life of man is a form of the Divine Will, and came into the created image of man from the Divine breathing-in <note>A reference to the "breath of life" in Genesis</note>. It is the formed Word of Divine Science <term>Wissenschafft (not modern science, but the "mirror" of God’s wisdom or his self-knowledge)</term>; however, it has been poisoned by the counter-breathing of the Devil and the wrath of temporal nature. Consequently, the will of life has formed itself with the external, earthly counter-image of mortal nature, and has moved from its perfect balance <term>temperamentum (the original state where all spiritual qualities are in harmony)</term> into a disharmony <note>original: "Schiedligkeit," a state of being divided or in conflict</note> of properties.

### On the Causes of Fear or Sadness / what Terror or Anxiety may be.

All sadness and fear, wherein a human being is terrified within themselves and feels afraid, comes from the soul. For the outer spirit, which comes from the stars <note>original: *Gestirn*; refers to the astrological and cosmic influences believed to shape physical life</note> and the elements, is not terrified, since it lives within its mother who gave birth to it <note>i.e., the physical, elemental world</note>: The poor soul, however, has entered into a strange lodging with Adam—namely, into the spirit of this world—where the beautiful creature is hidden and held in a dark dungeon.

The spirit of this world, however, has four lodgings in which the noble jewel <note>original: *Kleinod*; a common Böhmean metaphor for the precious, divine essence of the soul</note> stands locked away: Among these four, there is always one (and not all four) primarily manifest in a person, according to the four elements that every human has within them; and the person is themselves that same being—except for the soul, which is not of that same essence but lies imprisoned within it, and yet only one lodging and form among the four holds the chief rule over life. These four are called: 1. Choleric, 2. Sanguine, 3. Phlegmatic, and 4. Melancholic. <term>Complexions</term> <note>Based on the ancient theory of the Four Humors, Böhme uses these categories to describe how a person's physical and psychological makeup affects their spiritual journey.</note>

# Of the Four Temperaments

[He] recognizes this; he sprinkles sugar and ascribes piety to the soul only until he can lead it back into the **temperament** <term>Complexion; the physical and psychological disposition of a person</term>, so that it may once again eat the bread of sorrow.

O, how craftily he deals with the soul, just as a bird-catcher stalks birds! He terrifies it during its prayer (especially at night, when it is dark) and casts his **imagination** <note>original: "Imagination"; in Böhme’s theology, this is the power of the mind to "form" or "image" a reality, which the Devil uses to project false fears</note> into it, so that the soul thinks God's wrath is upon it and wishes to overthrow it. He always acts as if he had power over the soul, as if it were his own, yet he has not the power of a single hair over it, unless the soul itself despairs and surrenders to him. He is permitted to neither touch nor possess it spiritually; he only shoots into it with his **imagination** through the **temperament**.

This is the reason why he attacks this soul so: the chamber of the **temperament** is dark. He cannot insert his **imagination** into the light; he can only do so through human sin. In this **temperament**, however, he can succeed; it is close to his own desire because this desire creates darkness, and fear dwells within it due to the rough earth <note>The Melancholic temperament was traditionally associated with the element of Earth, which Böhme views as a "harsh" or "dark" foundation compared to the light of the spirit</note>. Otherwise, he has no more right to a single spark within it than in any other temperament. He can accomplish nothing more with his **imagination** than to frighten a person and make them timid. Unless the soul itself despairs and yields to him, he merely leads it to the point where it might cast itself down; he is not allowed to throw it down—the soul must do that itself. The soul has free will; if it stands before the Devil and does not want what he wants, he does not even have the power to touch the outer, sinful body. He boasts—

# Treatise of Consolation

...and prayer be found: For it is the greatest jewel in this world; whoever finds it comes out of Babel <note>original: "Babel." In Böhme’s theology, Babel represents the state of spiritual confusion, hypocrisy, and the corrupt institutions of the world.</note>.

5. A Melancholic disposition <note>German: "Gemüthe," referring to the internal seat of emotions, mind, and spirit</note> should, with great earnestness, guard against drunkenness, so that the soul is not too heavily burdened with earthly power. For when the body is so loaded with drink, the earthly power of the beverage entirely occupies the Chamber of the Complexion <term>Complexion-Kammer: the internal "room" or state of one's physical and mental temperament</term>. Then the soul imagines into it, eats of the earthly agony <note>or "torment"</note>, ignites its fire with it, and rejoices somewhat in it. But when the power sinks again and fades—that is, when the person becomes sober again—the poor soul is as if it were cursed. For in that excessive earthly agony, it loses the Divine Imagination <term>Imagination: for Böhme, this is the soul's creative faculty to form itself into the image of God</term>, or desire; for **GOD's** Spirit will not dwell in an earthly imagination. Then remorse <note>original: "Reuel," an archaic form denoting a stinging regret or painful shame</note> arises in the soul, and it feels as if it were cursed. Thus, **GOD's** wrath sets itself against the soul, as if he would thrust it into the root, into the Center, into the darkness. Then the soul is anxious and seeks after its "drinking-brothers" again, so that it might once more have a fool’s joy. From this come those drunkards who bind one day to the next and plunge their souls into **GOD's** wrath and disgrace. This I say truly, as I have recognized deep in the Center of Nature <note>original Latin: "Centro Naturæ"</note> and in the Principle of Life <note>original Latin: "Principio des Lebens"</note>.

## 1. Concerning the Choleric Complexion.

The person who holds their best treasure—the noble soul—within a Choleric house <term>Cholerischen Hause: the spiritual framework of the choleric temperament, traditionally associated with the element of fire, heat, and the gall</term> should, above all things, practice humility. Otherwise, they stand in great danger. They would do well to pour water into the fire so that their noble image <note>In Böhme’s theology, the "image" is the divine likeness within the human soul that can be tarnished or "burned" by earthly passions.</note> is not ignited. For this temperament produces great pride <note>original: "Hoffart," implying a haughty, puffed-up arrogance.</note>, stubbornness, and sudden anger; such a person becomes highly exalted, feared, and placed in high positions, but is not dearly loved. This remains so unless the Water of God—which is noble humility—enters the fire; then the person becomes worthy of love and gives forth the first light of grace. For this "chamber" has its own particular luster in outward nature. It is not naturally humble, unless it has Jupiter or Venus in its sign of life <note>Böhme frequently blends theology with Renaissance astrology; Jupiter was seen as a benevolent, kingly influence, and Venus as an influence of love and beauty.</note>. Yet, even under Venus, this temperament has its own devil that plagues it day and night with unchastity. I say this as a warning: there is great danger in this complexion, much greater than in the Melancholic one.

### Of the Phlegmatic Complexion.

## Concerning the Phlegmatic Temperament.

Truth and righteousness would be a noble medicine for you: For otherwise, you are prone to be full of lies and care little for what you give out or take in. You poor soul, you have a perilous path to travel here through the Sea of Misery <note>original: "Jammer-Meer." A common Baroque-era metaphor for the world of earthly suffering and spiritual trial.</note> in this temperament; you are constantly defiled by the vices of words and deeds. Water has a bright luster within it and produces a reflection, yet it is a false mirror: Likewise, the poor soul in this temperament has an almost unjust mirror. For water takes everything into itself, whether it be evil or good; it holds it and becomes clouded by it.

It is the same with this temperament: It absorbs the poisonous rays of all the stars <note>In Böhme’s cosmology, the "stars" or "constellations" represent the external cosmic forces that influence the human mind and body.</note> and presents them as a mirror to the poor, imprisoned soul; the soul then bites into this reflection and carries out in the body those works which, in the temperament, are merely a <term>Magical Mirror</term> <note>In Böhme’s thought, the "Magical Mirror" is the faculty of imagination and reflection that can manifest internal thoughts into external reality.</note>.

O, what good, sweet words—like sweet water offered freely—yet they are full of bitter gall mixed in from the stars.

Almost no deceit is too great: lies are the cloak of hypocrisy, used to present oneself with a mirror-like shine; where good Christians are in <term>Babylon</term> <note>original: "Babel." Böhme uses this to describe the state of false, superficial Christianity and spiritual confusion.</note>, this hypocrisy exists and demands to be counted as divine service.

# Epistle of Jacob Böhme

[...of the Father's] / Christ’s Love-<term>Essence</term> <note>original: "Ens"; Böhme uses this term to describe the fundamental spiritual "being" or "substance" that gives a thing its reality.</note> / as it receives Christ’s flesh and blood into itself / then the tiny spark begins to become a great fire and light / so that it shines and glows within itself with beautiful virtues and good works / and lives in great patience amidst the vanity of this world / yet grows forth like a beautiful flower out of the wild earth.

43. We have a parable of this in the sun and the earth: if the sun did not shine upon the earth, no fruit would grow. But when the sun shines upon the earth and penetrates into the <term>essence</term> of the earth, the earth’s essence receives the sun’s power into itself. From this, a great hunger arises within the <term>being</term> <note>original: "Ente" / "Entis"; variants of the Latin "Ens," used here to describe the internal appetite of matter for spirit.</note> of the earth for the sun’s power; and this same hunger imprints the sun’s power into itself. From this hunger of the earth’s <term>being</term>—which reaches upward toward the sun’s essence—a plant is drawn out of the earth with a stalk. In this stalk, the sun’s essence and power rise upward through growth, and the sun, with its rays of light, becomes substantial within the essence of the earth in the stalk and the root. One sees how, through the influence of the sun and the stars in the <term>Spirit of the World</term> <note>original: "Spiritu Mundi"; in Böhme’s cosmology, this is the animating, astral soul of the physical universe that mediates between the heavens and the earth.</note>, a different body develops from the stalk than the root in the earth; how the stalk develops into a bud for a beautiful blossom and afterward leads to the fruit. One also sees how the sun afterward ripens this same fruit over time and makes it entirely lovely.

# Jacob Böhme’s
## Two Small Books
# Concerning Christ’s Testaments.

## Preface to the Reader / regarding how the Testaments
## of Christ must be fundamentally understood / rightly
## distributed / and worthily enjoyed.

## A Mirror for Teachers and Listeners.

->1.<-

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring floral and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>
Dear Christian Reader / these small books concerning the Testaments of Christ <note>original: *Testamenten*; Böhme uses this term to refer to the Sacraments—Holy Baptism and the Lord’s Supper—viewed as Christ's legacy or "last will."</note> are well worth contemplating in this present time / when people strive only over opinions : Mankind has wandered quite far from the right understanding / in that they wish to preserve Christ’s Testaments through disputing and the sword.

# The First Book.
## The I. Chapter.
### Concerning the Self-Contemplation of Reason / how it is accustomed to run in Creaturely Form / when it considers Christ, and His Testaments <note>The "Testaments" refer to the Sacraments, specifically Baptism and the Lord's Supper, which Böhme views as Christ’s legacy to the church.</note>.

->1.<-

All conflict and misunderstanding regarding the person of Christ and His bequeathed Testaments originates from straying creaturely reason <note>original: *Creatürlichen Vernunfft*; this refers to human intellect that is bound to the physical world and sensory logic, separate from divine revelation</note>, which desires to be a mistress over all beings <note>original: *Wesen*; this can mean essences, substances, or created things</note>. It looks only into the multiplicity of beings and into the distinctions between those beings, and in such contemplation, it only loses itself. It breaks away from its Center <note>original: *Centro*</note> or origin and scatters its senses in the multiplicity of things, so that they cannot see what their ground is from which they spring. Thus, in their confusion and wandering, they break off from their <term>Chaos</term> <note>In Böhme’s thought, "Chaos" does not mean disorder, but rather the "Unground" or the eternal, hidden potentiality—the "nothing" out of which God speaks everything into existence</note>—that is, from the eternal Word of God and from the eternal Divine Speaking. Yet, it is in this speaking Word that all beings stand with understanding, reason, and senses, and from which they take their ground and beginning.

2. For if the unfathomable, un-natural, un-creaturely God, as the eternal ONE, did not [speak] His WORD <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page.</note>

<summary>This page introduces the first chapter, arguing that religious strife over Christ and the Sacraments arises because human reason focuses on the variety of the physical world rather than the singular divine source. Böhme describes how the mind "scatters" itself when it disconnects from the eternal Word of God.</summary>

->4.<-

All visible and invisible beings, spiritual and physical, have taken their origin in the breathing-out of the eternal One, and they stand with their ground within it. ### The First Little Book of T. Chapter 1.

...he stands again in the first birth and is spoken out again by the **Eternal Word** into a **Divine Willing**. For everything (whose life and will desires or runs outside of the Ever-speaking Word) is outside of eternity and lives merely for the sake of time.

10. But because the **soul** has its origin in the eternal word as a power of the same, it cannot rest in temporal existence; instead, it seeks its own Mother <note>In this mystical context, the "Mother" refers to the divine source or the "Sophia," the spiritual womb from which the soul was originally birthed into creation</note>, who birthed it at the beginning of the **creature** and brought it into creaturely form. But its wandering away <note>original: *Ausgehen*; the soul's act of turning its attention and will outward toward the material world</note> causes it to be unable to find its Mother.

11. Therefore, all conflict regarding the divine mystery is a useless thing; it happens from the outside, outside of God, in one's own **sensuality** <term>Sinnlichkeit</term> <note>The realm of the five senses and worldly perception, which the author views as a distraction from internal spiritual truth</note>, where this sensuality observes itself in nature and in creaturely form. There is no concept, nor true understanding or knowledge of GOD, unless figurative reason <note>Reason that relies on mental images, symbols, and human logic rather than direct spiritual experience</note> abandons itself and sinks back with its own will into its **Center** <term>Centrum</term> from which it departed—back into the Ever-speaking Word of God—so that it may again receive that same speaking or breathing of GOD within itself. Then, through divine **science** <term>Scientz</term> <note>original: *Scientz*, from the Latin *scientia*; here meaning an infused, experiential spiritual insight rather than academic study</note> or **knowledge** <term>Wissenschafft</term>, it may speak that Word out into a distinct and sensory form, so that it might be a dwelling and **Temple of God**, wherein God’s will works, governs, and desires. Otherwise, there is no true knowledge of GOD and His essence.

12. For no spirit knows GOD, or His Word and will, unless God’s Word and will are already within it.

<summary>This page explains that the soul cannot find peace in the material world because its true origin is the Eternal Word. It argues that true knowledge of God comes not from external intellectual debate, but from the soul surrendering its self-will and returning to its divine internal center.</summary>

### Chapter 1. Of the Holy Baptism of Christ.

...infused [the great Divine Love] into our *soul-essence*, as well as into our flesh and blood; He broke the monstrous <note>original: *Monstrosischen*; refers to the distorted, non-divine shape the soul took after the Fall</note> will of the soul—that self-conceived, figurative, and false desire—as well as the devil’s *imagination* <note>In Böhme’s thought, "imagination" is the creative power of the mind or spirit to "image" or form itself into a specific state</note>, which he had introduced into humanity. He broke the soul's own will and desire, and with His love, He brought the false properties back into a balanced *temperament* <note>original: *Temperamentum*; the harmonious state where all spiritual qualities work in unity rather than conflict</note>. Thus, He became a death to the death that held us captive, so that the fierceness <note>original: *Grimm*; a technical term for the harsh, consuming quality of God’s fire when separated from His light and love</note> of death and its fragility must die away within this introduced love; and human life, through such love, might sprout anew with a new will and eternal life through Him.

25. This newly introduced love and grace gave itself into the very center of the shattering of human life—namely, into the dying of man—within the **Person of Christ**. He took the assumed human self-will into death with Him and broke it. And that human image, which the self-will (through its *imagination* and desire for selfhood) had made so coarse, and which it had turned from its first angelic likeness into such a *monstrosity* <note>original: *Monstrum*</note>, He allowed to hang upon the cross and be mocked. In this way, He bore the eternal mockery upon the cross—which humanity otherwise would have had to bear—and demonstrated openly before all angels and spirits how this great grace-filled love intended to break the desire introduced by the devil, as well as death itself. Through this newly introduced love, He intended to sprout forth through death, to lead human life out through death, and to transform the fierceness of God’s wrath into love.

When one wishes to light a fire, one must have a substance <note>original: *Wesen*; in this context, it means an "essence" or "being" that provides the underlying material for a process.</note> for it that is capable of receiving the fire. It must be a substance that contains an oil and water, or it does not burn. For even if one throws a stone into the fire, it does not burn in such a way that it produces a shining light. The soul is to be understood in the same way. 2. And thus the essence of the illuminated and watery gentleness has faded, and has been locked into such a hard, insoluble death.

3. This is now what **God** said to Adam:

### Chapter 2. Of the Holy Baptism of Christ.

In such a kindling, human **desire** <note>original: *Begierde*; in Böhme’s theology, this is the fundamental "hunger" or driving force of the soul</note> approached God through the covenant, and God's **imagination** <term>imagination: from the German *Einbildung*, meaning the power of the will to form or "image" itself into a substance</term> entered into the covenant. Thus the **Holy Fire** in the covenant stood against the wrath during the introduction of human desire into the sacrifice. God's imagination in His love-fire entered the covenant, and human imagination also entered the covenant through the sacrifice in the fire. For in the fire, God’s wrath was opposed, through which human imagination had to enter the covenant, thereby consuming the sin and impurity of the human desire that pressed toward God. Thus, in the covenant, the love-fire stood before the human desire. This love-fire accepted the human desire within the wrath-fire according to its purity.

29. As can be seen with Moses at Mount Sinai, where the Father's **property** <note>original: *Eigenschafft*; a specific quality or mode of God's manifestation</note> first revealed itself in the covenant out of the wrath-fire and demanded human righteousness—that man should walk in full obedience and purity before GOD and approach Him in purity through the sacrifice in the fire. If not, He would consume them in a curse through this wrath-fire. This was an image of how human **vanity** <note>original: *Eitelkeit*; refers to the corrupted, fragile, and empty nature of the fallen world</note> should and must be swept clean by God's wrath-fire. But within that same wrath-fire, the love-fire stood before him in the covenant in the sacrifice, as an image of Christ, and extinguished the wrath-fire, so that the soul's desire, with its prayer and will, could penetrate into God through this wrath-fire.

### Cap. 3. Of Christ’s Holy Baptism.

2. For the human body, which required baptism, was of the elements. If it were now to be baptized, the Covenant had first to give itself into an elemental medium—namely into the humanity of Christ—and sanctify that medium, so that the human being might be baptized through this medium.

stood in the ground. The **Love-fire** became substantial—that is, a heavenly flesh—and gave itself to the Father’s **wrath-fire** within the property of human life as a form of food, as a fuel for burning, in the same way that one gives a lovely balsam to a fire, so that the fire then gives off a lovely scent and power from this balsamic oil as it burns.

3. Thus the Father now smelled this lovely scent in humanity within the fire of the soul—a scent which He had previously smelled in the sacrifice through the prefiguration <note>original: *Vorbilde*; a symbolic type or foreshadowing of a future spiritual reality.</note>. For **Christ** was now the true High Priest, who offered to **God** His Father the pleasant sacrifice of the sweet scent in humanity, and reconciled the wrath in humanity. The Altar of God, upon which **Moses** once sacrificed, was now in the humanity of Christ; He sacrificed to God the sweet humanity from the heavenly **essence** <note>original: *Ens*; a philosophical and alchemical term referring to the fundamental being or core substance of a thing.</note>, together with the Adamical <note>Referring to the fallen, earthly nature inherited from Adam.</note> humanity, into His wrath-fire (which was burning in the Adamical humanity). Sin was blotted out in the Adamical flesh through the sweet heavenly flesh (as through the substantial Word of love, through **Jesus**, as God's greatest sweetness).

4. **God** introduced the sacrifice of **Moses**, as the reconciliation in the fire, into humanity, and made **Christ** out of **Moses** as the true High Priest, who sprinkled the altar—that is, the **fire-life**—with His holy blood, just as **Moses** did with the animal blood in the prefiguration.

# The Second Little Book of the Testaments. Chapter 2. 84

12. In that same opened **Paradisiacal ground** <note>The "Paradisiacal ground" refers to the inner spiritual foundation of a person that was closed by the Fall but reopened through Christ.</note>, Christ remains dwelling in the light as the **Divine Love-<term>Ens</term>** <note>original: "Liebe-Ens". "Ens" is a Latin term for "essence" or "being." In this context, it describes Christ as the actual substance of divine love.</note>. For the power within the light is the Divine Essence, acting as the supernatural, **heavenly flesh**, a **<term>tincture</term>** <note>In the language of 17th-century spiritual alchemy, a "tincture" is a subtle, transformative substance that changes the quality of whatever it touches, much like a dye or a medicinal extract.</note> of life, which [tincture] permeates the soul and grants the **soul-fire** a holy, fiery radiance. However, let this be understood correctly: The soul is the "fire" of the Father; it takes into itself (as if into its own fiery desire) the essential love of the Son. This is the holy love-fire which has transformed itself into a **human tincture**, into flesh and blood (seeping into that same human life-power). In this way, the transformation of the soul’s will occurs.

13. Thus, we see this symbolized, first, in the **propitiatory sacrifice of Moses** <note>referring to the Old Testament "Sühn-Opfer" or atonement offerings</note>: the soul, acting as the "desire of faith" emerging from within the person, introduced itself into the sacrifice as if into an essence. It entered into the fire along with that essence; there, reconciliation through the fire occurred within the introduced covenant of the love-fire. This happened in the same way that the essential love of Christ was to give itself as food and reconciliation to the soul-fire, in which God’s wrath was burning. Second, we also see in Moses how the soul was not only **ransomed** <note>original: "ranzioniret", from the French 'rançonner', meaning to pay a ransom or redeem.</note> from sins through the fire and fed with love in the covenant with the holy fire of grace, but they also blessed the bread and meat through the reconciliation of the **Covenant of Grace** and ate it as holy bread and meat, just as God had commanded them.

### The III. Chapter.

## How Christ’s disciples ate and drank Christ’s flesh and blood, and how this is properly to be understood.

->1.<-

Reason should here move from **figurative language** <note>original: "Bildligkeit." Literally "image-likeness," referring to symbolic or metaphorical descriptions.</note> into the **non-figurative** <note>original: "Unbildliche." Referring to the actual, essential reality behind a symbol.</note>, and leave behind the folly over which men argue: For it was not a figurative partaking, but rather it is understood under a figure. Christ did not give his disciples his formed, creaturely, external, tangible, fleshly humanity—as if it were a piece of the same. No, that is not the case, for He sat with them at the table and did not tear apart the formed being of His body; rather, He gave them the **spiritual humanity** <note>In this mystical theology, Christ is seen as having a "heavenly corporeality" that can be shared spiritually without diminishing his physical presence.</note>, as the power of His body and blood—His own **mumia** <term>Mumia: A term used in 17th-century alchemy and theology (notably by Jacob Böhme and Paracelsus) to describe the vital, spiritual "balsam" or life-essence of a body. It is the spiritual substance that gives the physical body life and can be communicated to others.</term>, in which the Divine and Human power is comprised. This *mumia* is a true human essence of flesh and blood, and is a **spiritual flesh**, from which the visible image grows, and it is entirely one with the visible image.

->2.<-

Look at a comparison in the sun: the sun remains in its place, yet it penetrates with its radiance, power, and whole being, with all that it possesses in **essence** <term>Essentz (Essence): The fundamental spiritual substance or "being" of a thing, as opposed to its outward, material form.</term>...

## Chapter III.

# How the disciples of Christ ate and drank Christ’s flesh and blood, and how this is properly to be understood.

---

->1.<-

Reason should here go from the figurative into the non-figurative, and leave behind the folly about which men contend: For it was not a figurative partaking <note>original: "Niessung." A central term in Böhme’s theology of the Sacraments, suggesting an instrument or bridge between the physical and spiritual realms.</note> for it, just as the earthly **mouth** is only a **means** of the spirit. The spiritual **mouth of faith** of **man** grasps **Christ's flesh** and **blood** under **bread** and **wine**: not sticking *inside* the **bread** and **wine**. For **bread** and **wine** do not transform into **Christ's flesh** and **blood**, but they are the ordained **means** which (**means**) belong to the visible **man**, through which (**means**) the Invisible gives itself to the invisible spiritual **man**.

23. In **bread** and **wine**, two properties are understood: first (1), the coarse, elemental, earthly being, which belongs to the mortal human; and second (2), the power within, wherein the **Tincture** <note>original: "Tincktur." In Böhme's mystical chemistry, a Tincture is a spiritual life-force or "light-essence" that can penetrate and transform physical matter.</note> of the **bread** and **wine** lies. This **Tincture** exists above the elemental being, for within it the four elements lie in **Temperament** <note>original: "Temperamento." A state of perfect balance where the conflicting qualities of heat, cold, dryness, and moisture are harmonized.</note>; it is a heavenly, **paradisical power**. This same **Tincture** of **bread** and **wine** is the true **medium** <note>original: "Mittel."</note> by which **Christ** gives Himself to the human **tincture**, which is the human life. For man does not live by the four elements alone, **Matthew 4:4**. The coarse food which enters the mouth does not alone sustain life, but rather the inward power, the **Fifth Essence** <term>Quintessence: In alchemy, the "fifth element" or purest part of a substance that transcends the four physical elements.</term>, wherein the **Tincture** lies as a spiritual fire.

24. Elemental food produces only mortal flesh and provides a stirring or movement for the mortal life; but the spiritual man takes his **sustenance** <note>original: "Nutriment."</note> from the **Tincture**, for he is himself a **Tincture**, being a spiritual fire. Therefore, **Christ** infuses His **heavenly flesh and blood**—as the **Holy Anointing Oil**—into the life of man through and with the **sustenance** of the true life: that is, through the **Tincture** of **bread** and **wine**. This is not to be understood as if it were possible for the **Tincture** of **bread** and **wine** to physically grasp such things; rather, it is only a **conducting medium** for it, just as the outer mouth of man is only a **means** through which the power of the **Tincture** is infused into the food of the spiritual man.

### Admonition to the Reader.

## The I. Chapter.

# How Reason is Wont to Gaze in Creaturely Imagining When it Contemplates Christ and His Testaments.

### From Whence the Strife Concerning Christ’s Testaments Arises: How the Same is a Vain and Useless Thing.

<image-desc>Large ornamental woodcut initial 'A' featuring floral motifs and a central pedestal-like design.</image-desc>

**A**ll strife and misunderstanding concerning Christ’s person, office, and essence, as well as His bequeathed **Testaments** <note>original: "Testamenta." The Latin plural for "Testaments," referring specifically to the Sacraments of Baptism and the Holy Supper.</note>—within which He works presentially—arises from deviated creaturely Reason. This Reason wanders only in pictorial opinions and does not reach the ground of such a mystery; yet it wishes to be a mistress over all beings, wishes to judge everything, and merely loses itself in such imagining. It breaks away from its **Center** <term>Center</term> <note>original: "Centro." A Latin term for "center." In Böhme’s thought, the "center" is the divine point of origin; to leave the center is to fall into spiritual fragmentation.</note>, scatters the senses, and runs into multiplicity, whereby its ground is confused, the mind is disquieted, and it no longer knows itself.

No life can stand in certainty unless it remains in its **Center**, from which it originated.

Because the soul then originated from God’s Word and Will, yet has entered into its own lust and desire for self-will: so it may in such...

All beginnings proceed from the eternal **One**, as from the **Trinity** <note>original: "Drey-Einheit."</note> of God, through the **out-breathing** <term>Out-breathing</term> <note>original: "Aushauchen." A central concept in Böhme’s theology where God "speaks" or "breathes" the world into existence, similar to the Latin *spiratio*. It describes the movement from the silent Unity of God into the multiplicity of creation.</note> or speaking of the Unity of God, just as a spring flows from its source. Through this outflow, the Unity introduces itself into a self-contemplation, a state of being found, and a state of feeling, toward its own self-shaping and formation.

All visible and invisible beings, both spiritual and physical, took their origin in the out-breathing of Divine Power, and are a **counter-image** <note>original: "Gegen-Bilde." A reflection or mirror-image that corresponds to the divine original but is distinct from it.</note> of the distinct will of God, and stand with their ground within it. For the beginning of all beings is nothing other than an *imagination* <note>original: "Imagination." In Böhme's specialized vocabulary, this is not "make-believe" but the formative, creative power of the will to shape itself into a specific form or "image."</note> of the flowed-out will of God, which has introduced itself into distinctness, formality, and figurativeness; therein lies the whole *creation* <note>original: "Creation."</note>, and every life stands likewise in its own re-out-breathing and counter-imaging.

Since, then, human life is an outflow and counter-image of Divine power, understanding, and knowledge, it is proper for the same to remain at its origin; otherwise, it loses Divine recognition, power, and knowledge, and introduces itself through its own *speculation* <note>original: "Speculation." Here used to mean intellectual theorizing or mental wandering detached from the divine source.</note> into its own *centers* <note>original: "Centra." Plural of *centrum*. These are the internal points of focus or self-made origins that compete with the one true Divine Center.</note> and foreign formations, whereby its origin becomes darkened and foreign to it.

If one lives in God and wills with God, what need has he to dispute <term>dispute: formal theological debate or argumentation, often seen by Böhme as a distraction from inner faith</term> about God—where or what God is?

That he disputes about it is a sign that he has never yet felt Him in his senses <note>original: "Sinnen." In this context, Böhme refers to both the physical senses and the internal "spiritual senses" of the soul.</note> and is not surrendered to Him, so that God may be in him and will as he wills. It is a certain sign that he wishes to elevate his own opinion and images <term>images: mental constructs or rigid doctrines created by human reason rather than divine revelation</term> over others, and desires to rule.

People should confer <note>original: "conferiren," from the Latin *conferre*, meaning to bring together ideas or discuss.</note> kindly with one another, and each should offer his gift and knowledge <note>original: "Erkentniß." The state of being trapped in one's own ego-driven perspective.</note> as if they could not err. For we have a mighty enemy against us, who quickly leads human senses into strange images and makes man defiant. From this, sects and schisms arise.

It does not depend on specific persons, where one thinks that Divine understanding must come from them alone; for the Scripture says: "Test all things, hold fast to that which is good." (1 Thessalonians 5:21).

# The First Chapter.

When reason <note>original: "Vernunfft." For Böhme, "reason" is the logical, earthly part of the human mind that analyzes the physical world but is blind to spiritual mysteries until enlightened by God.</note> considers *Christ* and his *Testaments* <term>Testaments: a term Böhme uses for the sacraments (Baptism and the Lord's Supper), viewed as the sacred legacy and covenant left by Christ.</term> and thinks upon how *Christ* could be present in his *Testaments*, it imagines it occurs in a figurative <note>original: "bildlicher Art." Meaning symbolic or metaphorical, as opposed to a literal or substantial presence.</note> manner.

And when it realizes that it does not happen in a figurative manner, it falls away from the truth entirely and thinks he is present only in the *memory*; as when his Word is preached, reason thinks he only works powerfully within that Word. It thinks the same of his *Testaments*: that *Christ* works only spiritually in *faith*, and that the *Testaments* are merely signs by which we should remember what he has done for us, and through which we should only proclaim his death and the shedding of his blood, and keep them as a powerful memory for our comfort.

Thus, reason understands nothing at all of the *Kingdom* of *Christ*, much less of his *Person*, nor of his *Office* <term>Office: the spiritual role and function of Christ as the mediator between God and humanity.</term>. For this reason, people *dispute* and contend over it, seeking to reach it through rational inquiry. All of this fails to reach the true *understanding*; for *Christ’s* *Testaments* are heavenly, and reason is (earthly) worldly. It seeks *Christ* within time, and when it cannot find him there according to its own power, it assumes he is present only to the senses which soar up to him in heaven. But such a thing would not renew the life and bring it back into **GOD**; it would not bring about the new birth <term>new birth: also called regeneration; the process by which a person's inner spirit is awakened and transformed by divine power.</term>.

All conflict arises because people do not understand that very heaven where *Christ* sits at the right hand of God—that he is in the world, and that the world is in heav-

## The II. Chapter.

->**Of the Covenant of God after the Fall:**<-
->**What the Fall of Man is, and how GOD**<-
->**bound Himself to him again: What Circumcision**<-
->**is in the Old Testament, and what**<-
->**Baptism is in the New?**<-

When one wishes to light a fire, one must have a substance for it that is capable of receiving fire. It must be a substance containing an oil and sulfur, or else it does not burn. For even if one throws a stone into the fire, it does not burn in such a way that it becomes a shining light. The same is to be understood regarding the poor soul: when it broke its desire away from God’s essence of love and gentleness—which essence was within it in the beginning, like a spiritual oil and water, while the soul itself was like a spiritual sulfur in which the light of God burned—it then led itself into its own selfish desire. Through this, it became enclosed like a hard stone and lost all its love and gentleness. It became like a burning sulfurous spirit <note>In the mystical philosophy of this era, sulfur represented the "fire" or "drive" of the soul, which becomes agonizing and dark without the "oil" of God's light to temper it.</note> that could not be helped unless the oil of Divine gentleness and love were poured into it once again.

For such an infusion into the human nature <note>original: "Eigenschafft," meaning the inherent properties or characteristics of a being.</note>, there had to be a **subject** <term>Subjectum: In this context, a "subject" is an underlying substance or a receptive vessel capable of holding and manifesting a higher power.</term> to serve as a means or a "counter-likeness" so that it might occur, into which also man’s

# Preface to the Reader:

We have not written this work for the irrational animals who have the outward form of humans, but in their <term>likeness</term> <note>original: "Bildnuß." This can mean a likeness, an analogy, or a symbolic comparison.</note>.

### Chapter I.

<meta>catchword: Seeing/</meta>

...does not burn / that is there / and is not there: it is not a spirit / but rather a form of a spirit / like the <term>shadow-reflection</term> <note>original: "Schimen." This refers to an appearance, phantom, or reflection that looks real but lacks independent substance.</note> in the mirror / where every form of a spirit / shadow or mirror is perceived / and yet it is nothing / that the eye or mirror sees / but rather its seeing is within itself / for there is nothing before it / that would be deeper. It is like a mirror / which is a container of the sight of nature / yet does not grasp nature / nor does nature grasp the shadow of the image in the mirror. Thus one is free from the other / and yet the mirror is truly the container of the image; It holds the image / and yet is powerless against the shadow / for it cannot retain the shadow: For when the image steps away from the mirror / then the mirror is a bright <term>luster</term> <note>original: "Glast." Thus this is for us to recognize / and to understand of the eternal truth of God / which likens itself to an eternal eye without being; It is the <term>Abyss</term> <note>original: "Ungrund." The hostile torment has remained behind in the fire, and continues beneath the fire, in the cause of the fire, as in the wrathful anger.
